speechtext:
I intend to speak on two or three of the items mentioned in the resolution moved by the hon. member for Broadview. The first item to which I shall refer is forestry. Last fall I made a survey of a number of forestry camps which had been opened up in the United States I wanted to find out how they were organized and the calibre and standing of the young men in the camps. I must confess that I was more than pleased with what I saw being done in the camps I visited. The young men selected for these camps are the sons of men on relief living in the respective towns and cities from which they come. Their ages run from sixteen to eighteen years. Each camp consists of 206 young men, and sixteen local men, generally men on relief, are chosen to instruct and advise the young men on the work they are to do in any particular camp. The local men are supposed to have a knowledge of whatever is to be done by that camp- ditching, road work, or forestry work. In addition to the sixteen men who might be called instructors or foremen, there are two military men, retired and on the reserve list. During the working hours of the camp all the men in it are under the control of civilians, but after hours they are under the control of the military men. In the evening they are instructed in the ways of life; they are taught how best to get along in life. I took great interest in that. In one camp I visited, a batch of young men had just arrived-perhaps about thirty-five or forty- and I was struck with the apparent lack of discipline among these young fellows. Perhaps I should not speak of incivility, but I might say that there was a lack of courtesy in their general demeanour. The gentleman who was showing me around told me that these young men had just arrived; "and now I will take you to a camp where young men have been in training for three months," he said. There was a great transformation visible in the general demeanour of these other men. I was highly pleased with this second group of young men who had been in training for three months. They were very civil, they were courteous, and they gave ample evidence of their training. The instructors told me that at night they taught these men along various lines, and in the daytime they were instructed in the work they had to do.
I found that forestry, the replanting of trees and reforestation was apparently one of the primary objectives of the government at Washington. After visiting the camps I went to Washington to interview the Interior department, where I talked with heads of the

forestry branch. There I learned a good deal about the object they have in view.
The whole of the territory adjacent to the great lakes in particular has been deforested to an alarming extent since 1830. There I saw figures that indicated that in 1830 the estimate of standing timber in the state of Michigan alone was 150 billion feet, and by 1880 it had been reduced, by fire or by wanton destruction, but principally by the cutting down of timber, to approximately 35 billion feet of standing timber, board measure. In 1903 in the state of Michigan 500 million feet board measure were cut down in lumbering. The result of deforestation has had a tremendous effect on the water levels of the great lakes. In connection with the water levels of the great lakes, a subject which I shall discuss more extensively at a later date in the session, I believe that the Canadian government has a great work to perform. Anyone visiting northern Ontario, Muskoka, Parry Sound, on our own side of the line, will find just as great a deforestation as there has been in Michigan. The effect of that vast deforestation adjacent to the great lakes, in both the United States and Canada, according to a very eminent engineer who has written on the subject, Mr. R. E. Horton, has been a reduction in the rainfall on the whole St. Lawrence-Great Lakes area, of from three to eight per cent; and the concrete effect on the lowering of the water level on our great lakes, it is stated, has been a lowering of lake levels of from five to eight inches. Anyone can calculate what a tremendous volume of water that represents; we may get a proper idea of it by considering lakes Huron and Michigan, which are on the same level and are adjacent. Their combined area is 45,000 square miles.
I believe that the government has the ability to deal with the situation. I have great regard for a number of the ministers of the present government, in whose ability I have faith; and if they fully realize the menace involved in the lowering of the water levels of the. great lakes, to the extent that it has been going on, one way in which they can make a great national investment in this connection is through reforestation. In the United States there are 2,427 camps, and there are already in these camps approximately 500,000 young men. These men are paid $30 a month. Thousands of them have been used in the work of reforestation. If we followed a similar scheme, thousands of the young men in this country could be put to work similarly. The salary, I grant, is small, $30 per month, but these men get their keep and clothing and a certain amount of education; and if

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. MacNicol
they were not there they would be on the street comers-and anything is better than that. When they go into the camps they agree to send to their parents on relief $22 a month out of the $30 they receive. In Washington I saw figures showing that 80 per cent of these young men sent home an average of $25 per month to their parents.
Many of the men later find positions. I learned from the chamber of commerce that there is on the part of the firms associated with that institution quite a demand for the young men trained in these camps, because people know that they will be civil and energetic and will have had the benefit of a certain amount of training. It is stated that thirty-nine per cent of the young men enrolled in these camps receive positions outside the camps. The enrolment is for a period initially of six months, and they are allowed two additional periods of six months, or a total of eighteen months in all. I was informed that the maximum of young men discharged from the camps for not behaving themselves was less than five per cent.
I am convinced that the government has a great opportunity to perform a national work and to take a step towards raising the water levels of the great lakes by means of reforestation on our side of the line; the United States, I have no doubt, would take care of its side if there were collaboration.
Other speakers have referred to the young men. I am very greatly concerned about the young men in this country, for we have as fine a young manhood in Canada as can be found anywhere in the world. When the members of this house-at any rate those past forty-were young men there were jobs of various kinds for aJll; I can remember that when I was a young lad there were numerous jobs open. The young men to-day are up against it; they have nothing to do; they cannot possibly get positions. But they all have in their hearts the same desire that we had when we were young men; they want to do something for their parents. They cannot get anything to do, however. I take great interest in the young men, and it has been my happy privilege to assist many. But I regret my inability to serve them in the way of obtaining positions for them as I would like to do. It is a tragedy. These young men might be far better engaged in whart I believe is a great national work, the reforestation of deforested land that surrounds the great lakes watershed, than in doing nothing. For doing that they would not receive what might be called a dole; they would receive a certain amount of wages for rendering very
necessary and efficient service. Something has to be done to restore these water levels. When the subject is up later I will go into it more elaborately.
The hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) referred to Great Britain. Anybody who has been to that country within the last few years will be fairly well informed as to why Great Britain is coming back. Britain abandoned the free trade fallacy that is advocated in this country ,as well as in some other countries; all over England I saw, upon my visit a few years ago, factories that appeared to be th( better part of a mile long, and there are hundreds going up. If one goes to Manchester and to Birmingham, particularly, they will find great areas of factories that have been erected in the last few years, factories that are now making for Great Britain what was formerly imported into that country, principally from continental Europe.
I am tremendously concerned with the trade agreement that this government has entered into with our cousins to the south. In my time I have had much to do with industry and have visited many factories. I called on some recently, and in several cases I found that quite a number of employees have been laid off. How far that process is going to continue I do not know at the moment, but I cannot for the life of me see how Canadians can be helped by importing millions of dollars' worth of manufactured articles from our cousins to the south for use in Canada and at the same time displacing Canadians in our cities and towns who could have work making these same lines of material. If, as the previous speaker said, England is coming back-and certainly it is-and we know the reason, why does our own government depart from that same line of reasoning and lower the bars to admit into this country millions of dollars' worth of manufactured products that could be made by Canadians here in Canada?
If the government goes on with a program of public works I trust that some regulation will be enacted to prevent "chiselling" in connection with construction in the cities. I cannot quote them at the moment, but a number of cases have come to my attention where men on relief were compelled to work for a few days a week at a lower rate of wages than that at which otherwise they would have worked; that is what they call chiselling. The various trades, carpenters, bricklayers and others who work on the construction of buildings, should not be up against the temptation of chiselling and should not be encouraged to do so in order to obtain a few days' work per
234	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. MacNicol
week. In adopting regulations along this line, I hope the government will see to it that labour receives its fair and just reward for service rendered.
There is another angle to it. I am convinced that industry never again in our time will get back to the former number of working days per week. I am convinced that before very long five days a week will be the maximum not only in this country but in other countries. In that manner more men will be given employment. It will then be the duty of the authorities to find something for them to do in their leisure hours, on Saturdays. I recently paid a visit to Rouge River, a suburb of Detroit, where the great works of the Ford Motor Company are located. I was informed the property belonging to the company occupies 11,000 acres. I was taken over a considerable acreage.-I have forgotten the size-which contained thousands of small gardens, and on asking for information I was informed that, as the company was operating on a five day week basis, it had taken steps to provide land so that every employee who desired might have land to work on on Saturdays. I cannot help but feel that something like that has to come here before very long, that owing to shorter work days, which will likely be the rule in the future, men should be provided with an opportunity to grow things. In connection with that, and having served in industry a long time, I am convinced that few men over fifty years of age will again obtain jobs unless former employers feel disposed to take them back. We have to provide for many men who are over fifty years of age, and I know of no better way, when factories do not want them, than to provide land on which they can raise what they require for themselves; and if there should be any surplus they would have the opportunity to dispose of it in the adjacent cities. I believe that the government have a great opportunity in the very kernel of the resolution moved by the hon. member for Broadview if they take it wholeheartedly into consideration.
There is one other item of the resolution about which I should like to say a word, although I do not know how it should be handled. During the last few months many of the people I represent have lost or are very near to losing their homes owing to the high rate of interest and their inability to keep up payments. I believe that it is the duty not only of the federal but of the provincial governments to make an honest effort to do something worth while in this connection. There is no use fiddling while Rome

burns; we must do something worth while to stop the conflagration. Men have put their little all, saved over many years, into their homes, and have lost it. I do not know whether anything can be done to help those who have lost their homes, but surely something can be done for those who are on their way to losing them. ' How interest can be lowered I do not know. How arrangements can be made to save their homes I do not know. But it presents a great problem, and it is one that it is the duty of this government and the other governments to wrestle with. The homes of the common people in the cities are just as worthy of protection as are the farms in the country. We have heard in this ihouse a lot about farming, and I for one believe in giving the farmers more than is coming to them; I would almost go so far as to say that I would compensate them for staying on their farms. But a city has its problems too and one of the greatest, perhaps, is the saving of the homes of the average workingmen. A few days ago someone spoke in this house of conditions on the farms of the west. I could tell tales from now until next Christmas, if I wished, with respect to conditions in the dities, but that would not help anyone or do any good. I know the government are seized of the importance of the matter. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has had a good deal of experience. He has come up from the bottom; he should be qualified, and I believe he is qualified, to wrestle with problems of that kind, and I look forward to something along that line being done. Representing as I do a riding of sixty-five or seventy thousand people, many of whom are out of work and in jeopardy of losing their homes,
I appeal to the Minister of Finance, who is going to be in office for four or five years-[DOT] provided the government does not go to the country in the meantime-to do something in this direction. The problem is an important one. Do something for the workingmen in the cities and towns. They are just as worthy of consideration, in the saving of their homes and in the lowering of interest rates, as are the farmers. Do something to help the man in the city to save his home. If he cannot be given work, this opens up another method of helping him.
Let me conclude with what I said in opening,. in reference to reforestation. There is an opportunity for the young man, if there is nothing else for him to do. He can render splendid service there. I repeat this because I believe it worthy of repetition. The young man engaged in this work will do something for Canada; he will aid in

Reconstruction Policy-Miss Macphail
raising the water levels of the great lakes, the principal artery of trade and commerce by water for the eastern part of the continent of North America. I concur in what has been said by the hon. member for Broadview and only wish I could support him more effectively than I have been able to do.
Miss AGNES C. MAOPHAIL (Grey-Bruce):	Mr. Speaker, I desire to speak very
briefly on the resolution offered by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). Before doing so, however, may I say how much I appreciate the work done by the hon. member for Broadview in this house. This is by no means the first time the hon. member has brought forward resolutions having to do with subjects that are of interest to the people of Canada.
I am interested in each part of the resolution, though I do not intend to speak to each part. I have often wondered why, when there is the need for better housing, for the renovation of existing buildings, and for reforestation, we have not done all these things before now. We have the need; we have the material; we have the skilled and unskilled workers necessary, and all that is required is to bring these together. The essentials for doing so are credit, or money, and leadership by the federal government, but I believe we are going to see more public projects in the future than we have seen in the past. There has been a beginning in housing already.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that if we are going to have such building projects as I hope we will have we should not forget the need for agricultural construction. It is very difficult for the agricultural people to come under any of the housing schemes yet devised; in fact it is impossible. If the housing or building scheme is to serve agriculture, then it must be extended to include agriculture so that if the farmers want new buildings they can secure money for that purpose at low interest rates. That should apply also if they want to repair existing buildings, because in Ontario the problem of the farmers is not so much the construction of new buildings as it is the roofing, renovating and extension of buildings already in existence. In Canada we have something like 728.000 farm homes, of which I believe hardly one does not need something done in the way of renovation, construction or extension. It is true that many farmers need new buildings, but they also need to be able to get money at low interest rates in order to make their present buildings of greater use to them.
Since the hon. member for Broadview and the hon. member who sits before me at the moment (Mr. MacNicol) have spoken in glowing terms of projects on the other side of the line,' I will venture to do the same.
I should have hesitated to do so otherwise, but now I am quite sure it is all right. I was extremely interested in two projects that are being carried on in the United States, and I think it worth while taking the time of the house to describe them briefly. We are all concerned with the number of young people, not only young men-though sometimes in listening to debates in this house I wonder if the whole population is composed of men-but young men and women of Canada who go part way or all the way through high school and then, at the end of that time, want to pursue their studies further but are unable to do so. Since in most cases they are unable to get jobs it would be very much better if they could pursue their studies further if they are qualified and ambitious. I feel that if something could be done to make it possible for these young men and women-some of them only boys and girls in years-to go to school it would for a time at least lessen the strain of unemployment. It might also-and we would hope it might-enable these young men and women to evolve a philosophy by which to live.
Under what is called the national youth administration the United States has started to do some things that I think we must soon begin to do also. Starting first with the students in the high schools, eight per cent of the total attendance of the high schools of the United States may be employed by the high schools to do various tasks at wages which range from $6 to $8 a month, the object being only to provide them with sufficient money to keep them in school. The work they have to do must be such as will not interfere with those already employed, like shall we say, the janitor. These students, however, may be set to work as assistants to the janitor, as waiters in cafes or cafeterias, as teachers' assistants or as stenographers for the teachers. I saw some beautiful projects that have been carried out in connection with the beautification of school grounds, under expert supervision, by students working under this plan. They have done much to encourage and plan inter-class sports, to build tennis courts and other sports grounds for schools, to repair books in the libraries, to assist with translations, if they were senior students, and in keeping the records of the schools.
It is true, of course, that whether or not this project works out well depends very largely
236	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Miss Macphail
upon the ingenuity and resourcefulness of the principal of the school. The principal of one college, not a high school, told me he had heard of a friend of his who had wired the president beseeching him to send ten tons of leaves, since those they had on their lawns were already worn out. I suppose it is true that some principals were unable to supply jobs which were purposeful and constructive, but on the other hand I think a great many were able to do so.
They carry that through into the universities as well. Twelve per cent of the total enrolments in universities may be students who have been recommended by high school authorities but who have not money sufficient to take them through the universities. For doing work of a higher type than that I have indicated, they are paid $15 a month, which is sufficient to enable them to stay at school. However, at least one-quarter of the twelve per cent must be students who have not been in college the year before. Students who have graduated with a bachelor of arts or some other degree, but who want to take up post graduate work, can do very valuable research work, for which they are paid $40 a month. In the different schools and colleges I visited, I asked many questions about this system and I believe it has done a great deal towards enabling ambitious students to continue their studies. Further, it has done something which I believe is necessary in Canada, and I am sure just as necessary in the United States, namely, combined the work of head and hand, and brought about a new respect for hand work. In Canada I believe we have been too prone to divide sharply the two spheres of activity. Too often there is a feeling that people who work with the hands are not capable of working with the head, and that people who rvork with the head are a bit too good to work with the hands. The plan I have indicated has done something towards breaking down this absurd notion.
There are other phases of national youth administration which possibly have not worked out as well or, because they require more resourcefulness, have not been tried as extensively. In some places however vocational guidance centres have been established, at which attempts are made to guide young men and women toward the studies in which they are most competent and toward work for which they will be best qualified. In order to afford them further assistance a system of apprenticeships has been set up, giving high school and university students an opportunity to get into the work they would like to do, and for which experts have decided they are qualified. Going

into apprenticeship they gain practical experience of the work of their choice. I do not know very much about how the system has worked out, having heard only general statements made by people who were not very closely connected with it.
I have thought for some time that something definite concerning scholarships should be done in Canada. Only lately a pamphlet was issued discussing the subject at length. I shall not cover again the ground indicated in the pamphlet, but it serves to illustrate the point that many countries have encouraged young people desiring to acquire higher education, and have provided them with the means of doing so. Unless Canada follows the procedure adopted by Great Britain, Japan, the United States, Australia, New Zealand and in another way Denmark, we are going to be placed in a very unfavourable light and naturally hinder our development.
One other point, although possibly not strictly proper at this time, might be mentioned. Three times in the last two years I visited the Louisiana state university and on each of my visits I heard professors talking about the possibility of having scholarships on much more extensive scale. This year they are launching what would seem to be a tremendous scheme. They are increasing their farm, which is already very large, to an area of 4,750 acres, and they are taking 1,000 students on it. A complicated plan, which at the moment I shall not describe, is involved, but briefly they work on the farm for one semester, taking two subjects in the evening classes at which the teaching is done by university professors, and the following semester they go to the camps and take the full course. These alternate between different camps. It seemed to me that it was a common sense arrangement. It may be too extensive, but it is a common sense plan.
I believe the resolution offered by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) has similar merit. In my view it is extremely important that we undertake projects like this. I think all hon. members realize that the relief camps now existing cannot long continue. The work given the men in the camps is not varied; some of it may be very useful, but the variety is limited and it is not very interesting. Almost no1 hope is held out to them. I think it would have been much better if from the beginning we had paid the men a living wage and to a greater extent put them on their own resources. The conditions under which they are living is in my opinion very bad for their morale. I believe a change will have to be made, and the resolution

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Coldwell
offered by the hon. member for Broadview offers a good basis for an ambitious and extensive program of public works. While we may. not now undertake it I believe that before very long we will do so. Unemployment is not to be cured, even if purchasing power were to come back to the 1929 level or beyond that point. Displacement of labour by machinery will make it impossible for us to absorb our unemployed in ordinary industry, and some great projects of a national character are bound to come.

subtopic: PROPOSED MEASURES IN RESPECT OF HOUSING, LAND SETTLEMENT, REFORESTATION,- YOUTH IN EDUCATION, INDUSTRY AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to express my appreciation for the opportunity that has been afforded us by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) to discuss this problem. I listened with a great deal of interest to the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which followed, and while this motion may not be pressed to a division, nevertheless I think it is well that we should have an opportunity of placing before the government our views on the matter. It is, of course, not a new problem.
I recollect that one of the first things I ever iieard about the present leader of this group, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), was in connection with a survey of housing and living conditions in western Canada. That was many years ago. Since then at various intervals we have had commissions sitting and placing before the people of Canada their conclusions regarding the housing situation.
May I point out that it is not merely a problem of housing; it is a problem of health. Overcrowded living conditions both in the country and in the urban communities mean ill health and large expenditures in sanitaria of various types throughout the dominion. I was looking up some records a few days ago and I found that as early as 1911 a report was submitted to the health department of the city of Toronto stating in part:
There are few conditions found in the slums of Europe or in the greater American cities that have not been revealed in the city of Toronto, the difference being only of degree, and the conditions of lesser degree to-day will, if not corrected, become those of greater degree to-morrow.
Then we have Sir Clifford Sifton saying this at Ottawa in 1916:
We are to-day reproducing some of the worst things that have characterized the old lands. We are getting slums in our cities. But we are doing worse than that. Apparently we are failing utterly to get to the root of the problem which makes slums.
And, Mr. Speaker, we have to get at the root of this problem, and, as I said the other
afternoon, the root of it is not something of recent planting or recent growth, but something that has been growing and developing during the years that have gone by. I might quote further from the records but I shall content myself with one more statement that was made in the 1935 report on housing and slum clearance for Montreal:
The elements of the population of Montreal which are now compelled to find their abode in the slums or near-slum areas are not large in proportion to the whole population of Montreal, nor are the slums of Montreal as bad as those of many north American cities. However, they constitute a heavy burden, and the fact that they are widely spread to-day and rapidly extending calls for serious effort towards what has been called ' the new day of housing.' The depression has brought the Montreal housing problem to an acute stage and has emphasized the unsoundness of our existing working class housing schemes.
May I add that I found myself in sympathy with the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) when he suggested that something had to be done for those who are to-day losing the homes which they occupy and which they have built. That problem is an exceptionally serious one throughout the length and breadth of Canada; seldom a day passes but I receive a letter from one of the many people whom I have met in the past few years asking me to advise them what they may or may not do in relation to the pressure that is being placed upon them, and I believe my experience is probably the same as that of many other hon. members.
A few moments ago I was quoting from old reports, but I have before me now one which is very recent, issued so recently that it bears upon it the name of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). It is a report issued by the bureau of statistics and deals with the seventh census of Canada, 1931, and the housing accommodation of the Canadian people. I would recommend to every member of the house a perusal of a copy of this analysis of the census returns on housing in Canada. I find on page 3 of the report this statement:
Nearly sixty per cent of Canadian households occupy from four to seven rooms, and almost twenty per cent live in three rooms or less. Only 3-5 per cent of households occupy more than ten rooms.
We have heard a great deal about the cities; what of the rural areas? This report is exceedingly interesting to me because it confirms some of the statements I made in the course of the discussion on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last week. It says:
Distribution of the number of rooms in homes throughout the prairie provinces is quite different from that in other parts of
238	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Coldwell
Canada, particularly in rural areas. Over sixty per cent of prairie rural homes contain four rooms or less, while the number of such homes in Ontario is less than 23 per cent. In Alberta and Saskatchewan there are more rural households occupying two rooms than in any other room group. Prairie urban areas also contain proportionately more small homes and a lower percentage of large homes than is found in eastern Canada, although the typical size is five rooms.
That gives some idea of housing conditions in the prairie provinces. It may be due in part, as the report says, to the fact that the prairie provinces have been more recently settled, but, Mr. Speaker, I would say that it is not only because of recent settlement but because of the wide areas that are more or less subjected to frost, crop failure and drought, and the large number of farms that have been established on submarginal land in areas that never should have been opened for settlement. I have seen conditions in the northern part of Saskatchewan that made one's heart bleed, people inhabiting homes, tiny log buildings, where there were no conveniences of any description. I remember just about a year ago I was speaking in the town of Spiritwood in northern Saskatchewan, and an English lady there came up to me and said, "Can't you do something to bring to the attention of the authorities the condition of the people in this area? I have just come from attending at the birth of a new baby, and in that home there was nothing but a mattress made of gunny sacking stuffed with straw, and the only cover the mother had was the heavy coat her husband wore around the barn." Those are conditions of real poverty. It may be said that that is an exceptional case. That may be so, but I have seen and heard of a number of such exceptional cases.
I quote further from the census report. It goes on to say of prairie dwellings:
The smaller prairie dwellings doubtless are associated with the relatively short time the western provinces have been settled. The accessibility and cost of building materials is another factor which appears to have exerted a considerable influence.
And yet the condition which I have just been describing is one which existed, not in the southern part, but in the northern part of Saskatchewan where there were mills and where lumber was comparatively cheap.
I find this, too, from the census report, that the large six-room dwelling is predominant in the maritime provinces and Ontario, where there is the least evidence of crowding, and, conversely, that in the iprairie provinces, where three-room and four-room dwellings predominate, there is definite evidence of in-

adequate living space, particularly in the rural areas. The report continues, referring to certain figures quoted:
From these figures it appears that the great majority of households of more than six persons was inadequately housed. The fact that this was true of Toronto is particularly significant, for space available per person in that city compared favourably with most other Canadian cities of over 30,000 population.
The report contained one statement that was particularly interesting to me as a former member of the municipal administration of the city of Regina. It says:
The amount of space per person in 1931 was characteristically less than one room in households paying $15 rent or less per month. In this rental group, the average number of rooms per person centred around 0-7 and 0-8 in the twenty largest Canadian cities, varying from the lowest average of 0-5 for Regina to as high as 1-2 for Victoria.
Conditions of overcrowding, therefore, are not confined wholly to the older communities like Montreal and Toronto, but are also particularly acute in newer western cities like Regina. Under conditions of relief and poverty, which now exist, suffering is becoming aggravated. In the years to come we shall suffer as a people from the ill health and poor physique of the rising generation which consequences such conditions are bound to bring about. The report ends with these words:
These facts do not furnish conclusive proof of crowded conditions where the number of rooms per iperson is less than one. There is good reason to believe, however, that families in which earnings average $14 per person, paying less than $15 per month rent, and living in less than one room per person, are inadequately housed. In 1931, there were 51,778 or 15-7 per cent of all tenant households in Canadian cities over 30,000, who were paying less than $15 per month rent, the majority of them averaging less than one room per person.
That is an independent analysis of the census returns made by our own bureau of statistics. This should place the problem squarely before the government at this particular time. I know the government has many difficulties, but we must make progress. I look around and I see raw materials such as clay, with brick works nearby lying unused and idle, il go into the forest areas and I see the noble spruce trees standing there while mills within easy reach are lying idle. I am reminded that the members of building trades are out of work, that skilled workmen are walking the streets seeking relief. We have the labour; we have the materials; we have the need; it seems to me that all we require is the initiative and the intelligence to work out a plan that will meet these con-

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Coldwell
ditions. I am not so much interested in balanced budgets as in a balanced human welfare.

subtopic: PROPOSED MEASURES IN RESPECT OF HOUSING, LAND SETTLEMENT, REFORESTATION,- YOUTH IN EDUCATION, INDUSTRY AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: What explanation can the hon. member give of the fact that people who have materials such as cheap lumber and other commodities do not build larger homes for themselves?

subtopic: PROPOSED MEASURES IN RESPECT OF HOUSING, LAND SETTLEMENT, REFORESTATION,- YOUTH IN EDUCATION, INDUSTRY AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: To begin with, the people who need the homes do not control the mills nor have they access to the hardware which is necessary. If they are going to build a log home, they endeavour to build it on a small scale because of their inability to purchase sufficient stoves to heat a larger building. The whole matter comes back to the basic defect in our economic system.

subtopic: PROPOSED MEASURES IN RESPECT OF HOUSING, LAND SETTLEMENT, REFORESTATION,- YOUTH IN EDUCATION, INDUSTRY AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It is not for lack of material for building?

subtopic: PROPOSED MEASURES IN RESPECT OF HOUSING, LAND SETTLEMENT, REFORESTATION,- YOUTH IN EDUCATION, INDUSTRY AND EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
No, it is not lack of material; it is not lack of ability to build and it is not lack of intelligence to turn our raw materials into buildings. The irfhole matter is an inherent defect in our present economic set-up which makes it impossible for them to do the things that they otherwise would do.
The resolution contains one or two other suggestions which I should like to discuss briefly. One is in connection with land settlement. It all depends upon how such land settlement is to be undertaken and for what purpose. I have before me a statement showing the condition of certain settlers who have been settled for a long time upon the land in the province from which I come. I should like to quote from a bulletin issued by the farm management department of the university of Saskatchewan in 1934. It reads:
Indebtedness continues to be a problem of great concern. To pay interest on the present farm debt of Saskatchewan would have required about four-fifths of all wheat available for sale from the 1933 crop; and for the payment of farm taxes two-fifths of this wheat.
In other words, for those two items alone, in 1933 it would have required six-fifths of all the wheat produced, twenty per cent more than was actually produced in Saskatchewan. Professors Allen and Hope go on to say:
From our survey of last summer information is now available concerning the debt of 238 farm owners located in some of the oldest farming districts of Saskatchewan, operating about 44,000 acres of land, of which 37,000 acres were used for crops and summer fallow. Twelve of these farmers were _ free from debt, the remaining 226 having obligations amounting to one and three-quarter millions of dollars, and averaging $7,686 per farm, or $7,298 for the 238 farms. For the 238 farmers this debt averaged $18.64 per acre of cropland. Since the
summer of 1931, because of crop failures, the debt per farm had increased by $1,414, or $707 per farm per year. Most of this debt (77 - 3 per cent) was associated with farm real estate, 39-3 per cent being in agreements of sale, and 38 per cent in farm mortgages. Chattel mortgages amounted to 2-7 per cent of the total; implement debts, 3-1 per cent; taxes unpaid, 3-3 per cent; bank obligations, 3 per cent; and miscellaneous debts, 10-6 per cent.
If we are going to embark upon a land settlement scheme, how can we expect that people taken from our cities, people who are not familiar with conditions as they exist, will be able to make a success when men of long experience, such as these, cannot? This report covers a number of municipalities, including, I believe, that of Scott, in which are located Yellow Grass, Milestone and Lang. This is one of the finest areas in southern Saskatchewan and yet those people have been unable to make a success of their agricultural activities. How can people without capital and without experience be expected to succeed?
I view with a good deal of misgiving the propaganda now appearing in the press in various parts of Canada in connection with a land settlement scheme and a new immigration policy. I see that the quota from central Europe has been doubled since the new government came into office and I deplore this action. A short time ago I noticed that General Hornby was endeavouring to persuade various counties in England, such as Derbyshire, to embark upon a migration policy under which British workers would take up land in various parts of Saskatchewan. I felt that the government of Canada should not only not lend any encouragement to such a scheme but should prevent the putting of it into effect, because our problems can only be greatly aggravated by it.
I know it is sometimes said that our western farmers have been extravagant; but if you travel over the prairies you will find the condition outlined in this census, showing what actually exists in the form of a home-often nothing but a thin board shack, tar papered, standing on the windswept prairie. And if you will go into that shack you will find few of the amenities of life, few comfortable chairs; it is heated by a primitive stove. Extravagance! Why, not even ordinary comfort.
People sometimes say that the prairie farmers bought automobiles. Well, in western Canada, with the long distances between town and town, between the village and the farm, the automobile is not a luxury but a necessity, and moreover it is a labour-saving device, because it enables the farmer to get from his farm quickly to town to secure whatever is
240	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Coldwell
needed. If you go into one of the villages or towns on Saturday night and see the. cars lined up along the sidewalk, you will find that many of them are rather ancient models, and most of them are of the cheapest make. Fords, Chevrolets and Plymouths are the cars you will find the farmers using mostly on our western plains.
We have been told too that they have-spent their money taking trips to California. I am fairly familiar with many farmers in some of our best areas, and I know that very few of them took such trips. But on that score. I may say in passing, that after a man and woman have lived on the windswept prairies for fifteen or twenty years they are entitled not only to a trip to California but to a tour round the world and back again, if they feel inclined to take it.
In the resolution there is mention of the problem of youth. I have been particularly interested in that problem because of my life work and my long association with young people. I have watched with a great deal of alarm and sorrow young people whom I have known, who have passed through my hands, who have graduated from high school, who have gone to university and returned. They are on the street corners to-day or they are in relief camps. We are utterly destroying the young people who are growing up. Last summer I had the privilege-I regard it as such-of meeting some of those young men, the relief camp trekkers, who came to Regina. I had been told before they arrived that they were rather a tough lot. I met many of them and found among them some young men of high school education, other young men of university education, even young men very much like my own boy, who is about twenty. True, there were a few of a different sort; but on the whole they were a very decent bunch of young men, youths who desired to place their problems squarely before the .people of this dominion and its government in the only way available to them.
Many of these young men feel that they are unwanted and forgotten, and if the government of Canada to-day can do something to institute a widespread public works program of housing, reforestation, building of roads and bridges, elimination of level crossings, and so on, then such young men may have an opportunity of at least feeling that they are of some use in the society in which they live. I remember speaking with some of the trekkers, a week or so before the regrettable riot; they were assuring me that there would be no trouble, but one young fellow said, "No;

I would not start any trouble at all, but if trouble started I would be there; for after all, Mr. Coldwell, what is the use of living if there is nothing for you to do?" And then another added, "I am twenty-four; I should like to be able to get a home and to choose the girl I should like to marry." That was a very natural and human, desire, and throughout the length and breadth of Canada today there are thousands of young men in exactly that position.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, we have a problem of housing; there are thousands of people living in one roomed shacks. Now we have the material; we have the skilled men; we have the sawmills and the brickyards and everything we require. All we need to do is to use the intelligence we have and we shall find ways of bringing all these things together so that we may improve the conditions under which our people live.
Briefly, I wanted to contribute something to the discussion, and I feel grateful to the hon. member who introduced this resolution, because it has given me that opportunity. I hope that the ministers of the crown will carefully consider the suggestions that have been made by various speakers this afternoon and will give effect to at least some of them in the present year.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour): I wish to express my own sense of obligation to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) and to others who have taken part in the discussion of this resolution this afternoon. It was the purpose of the resolution, I take it, to direct the attention of the house to the problem of unemployment and to advance certain proposals for dealing with the problem.
During the past week we have listened to many references to unemployment, and that was to be expected; the seriousness of the problem is self-evident. We should be forgetful of our duty as members if we sought in any way to minimize its importance. In much of our discussion of the question of unemployment, however, there has been a lack of any definite proposals for providing new employment, and I think the hon. member for Broadview is deserving of congratulations upon malting certain suggestions having in view the creation of work for those who are now unemployed.
Before discussing the terms of the resolution, perhaps I may be permitted to say a word about our approach and attitude to this problem of unemployment during the present

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Rogers
session. Behind some of the references to this question in recent days there has been a veiled imputation that the present administration has not been sufficiently impressed with the gravity and urgency of the problem. In every case however the only apparent ground for such a suggestion has been the failure of the government to adopt outright some [DOT] sovereign remedy advanced by some particular group or individual as the one and only path to economic recovery. Let me say, as one who has a special responsibility in relation to unemployment and relief, that members of the present administration are fully seized of the gravity of the problem, and are prepared to study carefully any and all proposals which have'as their object the amelioration of the hardship and distress which have been the lot of so many of our people during the past five years. If we appear to 'be indifferent to these special panaceas which are advocated by certain groups in the house, it is not through any suspicion of the motives behind them, nor through any lack of appreciation of the sincerity of those who propound them. In dealing with this whole question of unemployment it is well, I think, that we should begin this opening session of a new parliament with the recognition that all of us, regardless of our political affiliations, have as a common duty and a common objective the progressive reduction of unemployment and of its serious effects upon the fabric of our social and economic institutions. Our differences are not those of human sympathy, of compassion, or of social responsibility; they . relate rather to the methods by which we hope to achieve the object which we all have in common.
For more than five years we have been dealing with unemployment as an emergency situation. It came upon us almost unawares. Naturally the task of dealing with it became a very difficult and disagreeable duty. Our policies have been improvised quickly in response to immediate pressures, and there has been on the whole a conspicuous lack, I think, of objective study and adherence to fixed principles in the various measures we have adopted for the liquidation of unemployment and relief. In the case of the late administration I believe certain things were done which ought not to have 'been done, and certain things were left undone which ought to have been done. But no doubt that might have been said of any administration in power at that time. While recognizing fully the difficulties confronting the late administration, I think the course followed by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was 12739-16
more erratic than it need have been. That, however, is a question that can be discussed more properly at another time. I suggest now that we have reached a stage where it is possible and certainly desirable to take a careful inventory of our present situation, and either return to old principles or adopt new ones which are recommended by reason and confirmed by recent experiences of our own and other countries.
This is a very comprehensive resolution; it is framed in generous terms. For that I am grateful to the hon. member for Broadview. He could scarcely be brought to order for wandering from his subject, nor, I hope, shall I be brought to order for a similar reason. Much of the discussion hitherto has been concentrated upon one of his proposals, namely, that of housing. I propose simply to address myself to the first paragraph of his resolution, and instead of taking particular suggestions contained therein, to deal rather with some of the broad questions of policy which I believe are implied in his resolution.
The first question raised by the resolution is the utility of governmental expenditures as an aid to unemployment and a stimulus to economic recovery. Although the resolution does not state this in so many words, the phrase "national housing, building, reconstruction, renovation, slum clearance, land settlement hnd reforestation policy" suggests that what the hon. member has in mind is the provision of funds for this purpose out of the dominion treasury. Whenever in recent years a national scheme has been proposed, there has usually been behind it the thought that the dominion government should assume either a larger share of financial responsibility or full financial responsibility in carrying out such a scheme. Certain of these proposals will be within the memories of members present in the house. Associated with all such proposals, moreover, is the assumption that the dominion parliament, unlike other governmental agencies under the federal system, is possessed of unlimited resources to meet the costs of additional works projects. Undoubtedly there is some excuse for the prevalence of this view, and for the consequent pressure upon the dominion government to assume a steadily increasing share of financial responsibility for relief works of one description or another. The provinces and municipalities have restricted powers of taxation. The municipalities have restricted borrowing powers. There is no such legal restriction upon the taxing powers of the dominion, and none with respect to its borrowing powers. It is well to remember,

242	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Rogers
however, that while the dominion is not subject to any legal restriction upon its taxing and borrowing powers, it is subject at all times to what I might describe as a prudential limit in the exercise of both these powers. Moreover this prudential limit is not confined to the dominion parliament. It applies as well to provincial legislatures and to municipal councils. The hon. mem* ber for Broadview does not need to be reminded of this fact. He has served for several terms as chief magistrate of a great Canadian city, and he well knows that extravagance or misdirected expenditures may so increase the debt and tax rate of a municipality as to discourage commercial and industrial expansion through the natural channels of private and corporate investment. That consideration is one which we must at least have in mind in dealing with this problem which has been brought before us this afternoon.
If the mover of the resolution has in view the encouragement by governments of private investment in housing and building construction, I would support him wholeheartedly in his advocacy of such a policy. If he has in mind the close cooperation of dominion, provincial and municipal governments in slum clearance projects, I would agree with him that such a policy should receive the sympathetic examination of the various governments concerned. If, however, he proposes a scheme under which the dominion government should at this particular time assume an immediate or contingent liability in relation to any large scheme of this character, I would suggest that we should see our way very clearly before entering into any such commitment. I do not yield place to any hon. member in my desire to see slum clearance projects undertaken. I realize fully the social evils that follow in the train of slum and bad housing conditions. I feel, certainly, that we must do what lies within our power to remedy these conditions as soon as possible. I simply put it to the house at this time that in any long view of the problem we are compelled also to consider how far it is desirable to commit ourselves to large public expenditures if-and I shall deal with that point later-by so doing we discourage or deter the natural flow of savings into housing through private and corporate investment.
I submit this view, as I have said, not with any lack of sympathy for the object which the hon. member for Broadview has in mind, but solely because it seems to me that we have reached a point in the state of our public finances when we are compelled to consider

the deterrent effect of large governmental expenditures and increasing deficits upon the flow of savings into productive investments. Savings for investment are notoriously sensitive to conditions of public finance. The even flow of savings into private and corporate investments depends in very large measure upon confidence in the national credit. I do not believe in giving national credit precedence' over human need. To do that would be a gross perversion of the objects of government. We must all agree, I think, with Edmund Burke that the true purpose of government is the provision of human wants. Without exaggerating the importance of the national credit, however, this like every other government, is compelled to recognize the relationship between public finance and private investment if it is to discharge faithfully its duty to reduce unemployment by the encouragement of private enterprise and the steady promotion of production and exchange. We must go as far as we prudently can with public expenditure, but at all times we must keen in view the effect of mounting debts and unbalanced budgets upon the normal expam sion of private employment.
A moment ago the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggested that he was not particularly impressed with the importance of balanced budgets. I have already said that at all times human need must be the first end and purpose of government, but I do suggest that, circumstances being as they are, it is taking a short view of the duty of the government to the people of Canada to assume that we can continue with unbalanced budgets and at the same time expect the cooperation of private and corporate enterprise in supplying more employment in this country. I do not think it is possible for any government to spend its way out of unemployment by vast expenditures on public works. I am sure, however, that it is possible for a government to spend its way into chaos by a policy of this character, continued over a long period of time.

I think any government, no matter of what party, that takes control of the destinies of this nation should have a definite policy in this connection. What has happened? Seven months ago the house passed a housing act, giving to private capital the incentive to build homes in Canada. Have they built homes? Have they gone ahead with a construction scheme in any part of the dominion? Certainly not. From a report tabled this afternoon I find that the total of loans approved since the act became operative amounts to approximately two-thirds of a million dollars. That does not mean that construction has proceeded to the extent represented by that sum. In other words, the government of the day gave to the private loan companies money at four per cent as an incentive to build homes; twenty per cent of the value of the homes was to be mortgaged by the federal government at the rate of interest referred to. Private enterprise has got us into the chaos in which we find ourselves to-day, and now we are looking to private enterprise and initiative to get us out of it. I wish the hon. gentleman
would reserve those remarks for his own speech, and make his own speech in his own way. I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to tackle this problem it will have to be done by means of government money at a low rate of interest. In 1919 an act was passed in Canada with respect to housing, and that act I greatly prefer to the one passed in 1935. The unfortunate part of the 1919 act, however, was that when the money was loaned by the federal government to the provinces there was not sufficient federal supervision over the expenditure. In my opinion the government of the day ought to provide funds for housing purposes at a rate not exceeding three per cent. There is no reason why the government should not do so; I do not think there is any other self-liquidating project which governments can undertake than housing. The collateral in a housing scheme would be well worth the consideration of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) in collaboration with the officials of the Bank of Canada. If money were available at three per cent there would be witnessed a boom of construction right across the dominion; but if private mortgage companies are to loan the money at the rates they now ask of five or five and one-half per cent, then I am afraid very few houses will be built in this country.
The minister has said that the government realize their responsibility to the unemployed. I wonder to what extent they appreciate that responsibility. Is that responsibility discharged by the appointment of a commission to investigate matters that have already been many times investigated? I do not think that is the way to deal with the problem. The problem can be dealt with in one of two ways: either the government ought to

provide work, or, if it is not in a position to create employment by means of public works, then it ought to find other methods of increasing productive employment and distributing the work among those who are willing to perform a useful function in society. That would mean a drastic reduction in hours of labour and a notable increase in productive capacity, and when we have reached that stage of increasing productive capacity we ought also to increase the consumptive opportunities of the people in proper ratio. Whether the government will do that, I cannot say, but for the dim and distant future they have some policy of coping with the situation.
The minister admits that it is the duty of the government to reduce unemployment. Quite true; but what is there in his speech that would indicate what policy the government have for reducing unemployment? None whatsoever; and I think, as was indicated in the speech from the throne and as well this evening by the Minister of Labour, there is no greater responsibility that rests upon the government and this house than that of dealing definitely and without hesitation with this great and growing menace of unemployment in Canada.
The problem of youth has been mentioned -a very important aspect of our whole national problem. Was there a ray of hope for the youth of the country in the speech delivered by the minister? None at all, except the ultimate closing down of the camps. That is something regarding which I am in hearty agreement with the minister, but at the same time I should like to know what alternative there is for these young men when the camps are closed down. Again, we are told that if we only wait, if we only have patience, in the distant future we shall get some idea of what the government's policy is in this regard.
And then the minister wanted an inventory of the whole situation. I think we have a pretty good idea of what the situation is. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), speaking in the house last week, indicated that there were about 400,000 men out of work. If that was the estimate given, and if it is our duty as a parliament to -grapple with the problem of unemployment, wbat are we going to do with the 400.000 who are out of work at the present time? A section of them comprises the construction industry of this country, men engaged in the building trades, vast numbers of whom have not had a day's work probably for years. They had hopes and visions that by a comprehensive housing scheme something might be done on

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Heaps
their behalf. But no, not even a housing scheme is to be considered, because we have to take into consideration the financial standing of the country. Speaking this afternoon from his seat in the house, the first minister made what I may describe as an unusual kind of statement. It was very terse, .probably to the point, and I do not know whether it did not even contain .the semblance of a threat. He told the house that we have to consider the commitments of .parliament and that very soon these commitments will be submitted to the house, 'and he left the impression on my mind and probably on the minds of other hon. members that there was something in those commitments that would almost make our flesh creep when we knew the actual facts. He warned the house further that these private members' resolutions ought to be spoken to but not voted upon; that if we went so far as to vote on these motions, the question whether they were in order would have to be considered; that they were recommendations for money expenditures; that resolutions involving expenditures were the prerogative of the government, and that only a government member was allowed to bring in resolutions dealing with money expenditures. In other words, if we did not behave ourselves and if in particular the private members of the Liberal party did not behave themselves, they would not have the opportunity of even discussing these questions, because possibly they might be asked at some time on a point of order to vote against themselves and put a gag on themselves. I do not know whether I have correctly interpreted the statement that was made by the Prime Minister. If I have not, of course I will apologize to him.
There has been talk from the Liberal side of the house about clearance of the slums. So long as we have poverty we are going to have slum conditions; the two are inseparable. And while I am anxious and desire to see slum conditions ended as soon as possible, I think the cheapest and quickest way of doing away with slum conditions would be to build cheap homes, wholesome homes, homes that could be rented at a very low price, one within the reach of the average man who is compelled to work for wages. That means, of course, something fundamentally different from what we have hitherto done in the House of Commons. I realize it would be a complete departure from many things we have formerly done. I know of some municipalities that would be quite willing to undertake a scheme of this character if cheap money were available. When I say cheap .money I mean money at about three per cent; even at three per cent there
would be a good profit for those who handle the money end. After all, money can be handled by banks and similar institutions for, I think, one half of one per cent. All above one per cent is profit, for I know, with the housing schemes we had in. Winnipeg under the act of 1919, and a differential of one per cent between what the city was able to borrow the money at, and the rate the money was loaned to prospective owners of homes, the Winnipeg housing commission was able to show each year since the inception of the scheme, fourteen or fifteen years ago, a profit, even during the depression period, of about $12,000 to $14,000. So if money were available at three per cent, as compared with the six per cent that was paid for it in 1919 and 1920, I think a success could be made of any housing scheme.
I am extremely sorry to have observed the attitude which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has taken toward this particular issue this evening. I hoped, as others on this side of the house hoped, that he came into the house with some radical leanings. His speech this afternoon could have been given by a good Tory, and a "Tory would not have had to object to what he said. It was a type of speech which I did not expect from the Minister of Labour, because, having read some of his writings and known some of the things he preached in the past, I hoped for something better from him when he came to deal with labour problems. I know his heart is as sympathetic to the unemployed as my own or that of any other hon. member. It is not sympathy that the unemployed of the country are looking for at the present time; it is action, and action they have not received. There is all the difference in the world between the two. I want to see this government take action. I will support any measure that it proposes which means doing something toward solving or helping to solve the problem of unemployment. But the speech we listened to this afternoon contained very little in the way of encouragement for people who are out of work. I hope the slip the minister made this afternoon and this evening is just temporary. I think he has been awed somewhat by the newness of his surroundings. What the Prime Minister said this afternoon about the commitments of this country and the balancing of the budget must have overawed the Minister of Labour and got the better of his sympathies and even of his judgment.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North is sitting very close in the house to a group of men who I have no doubt are very sincere, but who have made promises which it will take them a very long time to live up to. The times of promises are passed. We are getting action from the present government.
I want to say a few complimentary words in regard to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), for giving the house an opportunity of speaking in a general way on matters pertaining to the nation as a whole, matters in which not only every hon. member but every citizen of this wonderful country are deeply interested at the moment. First of all I want to say a few words about housing. This is not a new thing in Canada. Immediately after the war, in 1919, a housing scheme was inaugurated, and we have the experience gained at that time to guide us now. That was not absolutely without flaws, however; no later than last Saturday I received a letter from a friend of mine, a good doctor who practises in the town of Cochrane, who built a house under that 1919 scheme. He told me that a writ was going to be issued for the sum of SI,225, representing back payment under that housing scheme, back interest and municipal taxes. In a word that man is going to lose his home, all because the scheme of 1919 was not properly studied, and because the costs of 'building material were too high. The same situation exists in many other cases. I was astonished to hear the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) say that the housing scheme had been a complete success in Winnipeg.

speechtext: Absolutely.

speechtext:
It was not a success in a good many cities and towns in Ontario.

I could mention many constituencies represented by hon. members in which there were many failures, and that applies perhaps more particularly to my section of the country. No doubt the late government took a step in the right direction last year in inaugurating a housing scheme; no doubt that scheme could be enlarged and improved, but that will never be done by promises or the waving of hands.
This afternoon the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton) mentioned that the housing scheme in England had been a huge success, and was one of the main reasons why Great Britain is on an even keel at the present time. That is only partly true; we all know there is a great difference of opinion among those who have studied the housing scheme in England and grave errors were made when that scheme was inaugurated, and the same applies to Canada. No doubt the discussion here to-day, which has been maintained on a very high plane, will bring about some good results. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Mac-phail) this afternoon rightly mentioned that the farmers and settlers of this country should also be included under any such scheme. It is all very well to visualize the slums of the big cities; it is easy to put our fingers on them. If it were possible, however, to get the poor little habitations of the rural sections of northern Ontario grouped together you would see much worse slum conditions than you have in any city of Canada, and I believe those people deserve consideration under any housing scheme.
In this connection we also ask the government whether it would not be possible to help the dwelling situation among our farmers by extending the operations of the farm loan act. In my files in my office in this building I have hundreds of letters from farmers who have their deeded land in northern Ontario and who have made application to the farm loan board. In ninety-nine cases out of a hundred they have been turned down, for no apparent reason at all. In some cases they received letters two or three months after their applications were filed; after that lapse of time their fees were returned and they were told that, after inspection, the government did not find it possible to loan them any money. I remember last year when the then Minister of Finance, presenting an amendment to the farm loan act, asked parliament to vote $90,000,000, and at that time he said that if this amount should become exhausted another $90,000,000 would be voted. We supported that measure with both hands, but I do not believe it has been of as much

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Bradette
benefit as it was expected to be. I will take another opportunity to place before parliament and the country the actual situation that has been created among the farmers of this land.
I should like also to say a very few words with regard to reforestation, with which I should like to combine the preservation of our forests. In the Ontario legislature, whether on the opposition or on the government side, I always maintained that the Ontario fire rangers should be employed all the year round. I believe the same principle that is applied to medicine should be applied to our forests, that prevention is better than cure. It should be possible to have thousands of our young men employed in the preservation of our forests during the dangerous time of the year, and to have those young men also employed in replanting and reforestation in every province of this confederation. I also fervently hope parliament and the government will find it possible to bring about fair prices for our forest products. It may be a revelation to a good many hon. members to learn that, except in the years 1917 and 1918, so far as northern Ontario is concerned there never has been a settler, a farmer or a small forest owner who has made any money out of forest production. The moment that you are able to create new markets or the moment you make it possible for these farmers to develop their own forest holdings at remunerative prices you will find that they will need very little protection, because they will see the advantage of looking after their holdings, and will husband every tree on their holdings.
I should like to say a few words also with regard to the land settlement scheme which has been, mentioned by the hon. member for Broadview. That is a moot question, not only in this but also in every other country throughout the civilized world. We realize that our civilization has tried to expand in only one way, industrially, and this statement applies with great force to Canada. Only two years ago I read an article in Saturday Night which asked whether it would not be better for Canada to become more and more an industrial rather than an agricultural country. As far as nature and climatic conditions are concerned, kind providence wants this to be primarily an agricultural country. That fact cannot be denied, but we have falsified the true state of affairs. See what has happened in this, as wel as in every other country, in the last twenty years. The young people from the rural communities have found their way to the urban centres, and to-day all governments are putting their
ears to the ground and thoroughly studying the agricultural situation, in an endeavour to get people to go back to the land.
I well remember when in 1930 the then Minister of Labour, who by the way is a personal friend and neighbour of mine, inaugurated a back to the land movement. I told the minister at that time that I was absolutely in favour of such a movement, but when in 1931 he told the House of Commons that thousands of people had been placed back on the land without the expenditure of public money from either the federal or the provincial treasury, I told him the thing was absolutely impossible. In that year, however, the government inaugurated the Gordon plan, and in very large measure I have upheld the principles of that plan. I believe in my riding this land settlement scheme has progressed further than in perhaps any other riding in Canada. I have hundreds of these people near Matheson, Iroquois Falls, Cochrane, Kapuskasing and Hearst. I am primarily a pioneer myself; I went to northern Ontario over thirty years ago, so I am reasonably familiar with the present situation. These were very fine people who were taken from their former surroundings under a movement inaugurated by the federal government and assisted by the provinces and municipalities, but their troubles are not over. It is true that the federal government, the provincial government and the municipality each contributed $200 to establish each family on the land, but let me remind the house that two years ago I told the then Prime Minister that when this money was spent these people would be worse off than they were before settling on the land, and that the federal government would find it necessary at the end of that period of time to continue to help these settlers. These people who have been affected by the back to the land movement are practically the wards of the present government. Many of them, unless help is given to them will have to give up what they have begun and lose the fruit of their work of the last three years. It will be found absolutely impossible for ninety-five per cent of them-and I make this statement deliberately-to get along, and they will have to get away from their present holdings. At the present time the municipalities have washed their hands of the situation, and the responsibility is placed on the door step of the federal government.
We are living in strenuous times. Sometimes we are astonished to hear statements such as that made by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), for example, who said only a few days ago in this House of
252	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Bradette
Commons that for the first time young people were represented in parliament. Surely he did not mean that. Surely a member of parliament worthy of the name represents not only the old and the young people in his constituency, but all classes including youth, middle age and old age. Every man sitting in the House of Commons is fully seized of the exact situation.
