speechtext:
They are certainly included, I must assure the hon. member, with great gusto, and I sincerely regret the involuntary omission. We are seized of the facts as to the serious situation of the people, and we all agree that if there is one class in full contact with all classes then certainly it is the members of parliament. I am leaving no one out of the picture. Each of us receives dozens of letters every day from people who are suffering. We do not throw these letters aside; we do not say that we represent only one class. We represent all classes of people, the whole population in our respective constituencies.
I shall have further opportunity to speak about the land settlement scheme, but there is one thing I should like to make clear: So far as northern Ontario is concerned we want no more people from southern Ontario, under either the Gordon or any other plan, until such time as we rationalize colonization and agriculture, and make the present occupants prosperous. Farming is a vocation; it is a calling from the heart. A man's inclination must be natural; he must be ready and willing to sacrifice if he is to become and remain a farmer. New people were brought to the land under these schemes, and the present holders of new sections in our own country, although they were courageous and enterprising, are not prosperous. The primary duty of a government, whether it be provincial or federal, is to render prosperous the actual settlers on the land. That would be the best possible kind of advertising, and the best possible scheme. I believe that principle could be easily applied. So far as I am concerned, using my own energy, directing my attention to the present provincial government in Toronto and also making application to the federal government, I believe we must of necessity rationalize our viewpoint and our policy, so far as colonization and agriculture in Canada are concerned.
I believe it would be worth while if the federal government would create a central fund whereby it would be possible to foster land clearing and ploughing. That would be the best possible way to keep our settlers off

the relief lists. In the past we have dealt artificially with our industries. Every one knows that we have exempted them from certain things, and have given them the protection of high tariff barriers, concessions, privileges and tax exemptions. During all this time, in most cases agriculture and colonization were left to themselves. To-day if we wish to have prosperity back in Canada we must deal properly with the primary producers, the farmers of this country. If they cannot be prosperous we can never have prosperity. That problem is possible of solution, because we are working with a class of people who are most reasonable, most thrifty and most industrious. All they want is a chance. They want a chance-not to have luxury, not to have great comforts, but only to have a decent living, and a chance to succeed.
I wish to make only one or two further observations which are in my mind at the present time and which can easily be coupled with the back to the land movement. I have spoken about immigration. I was highly elated this afternoon when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to immigration and stated that he was against it. At this time there is a movement on foot to bring in more fine people from some other lands. The time has not yet arrived for such a movement; I do not think it will arrive for many years to come and as far as I am personally concerned I never want it again. I know the rural situation, and I can well remember the protestations of the hon. member for Grey-Bruee (Miss Macphail) and other hon. members in the group to which she belongs when my party maintained an extensive policy of immigration years ago. Sitting in the far corner of the house, as a new member, I protested. No matter what any hon. member may have to say about bringing thousands of new immigrants to this country, I say that we have no place for them at the present time. What would we do for them? I remember a previous immigration, policy, when we had people coming from central Europe and from Great Britain. At that time we tried to put them on the land, but I wonder how many of them stayed there. Not two per cent of them stayed on the land. Ninety-eight per cent of them found their way to the industrial centres of Canada, and many reached the United States. I well remember the late Minister of Trade and Commerce, for whom I have the greatest respect, deploring the fact that our university graduates and craftsmen and artists could not find fruitful occupations in Canada, and had to go to the United States, a condition which was brought about to a

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Hayhurst
great extent by the immigration policy of the government. All parties in the past sinned in that regard, and I fervently hope that these actions will not recur.
Last fall I attended a meeting of a board of trade in northern Ontario. It was held in the Porcupine section, where at the present time we have the greatest gold mining development in the world. In that section thousands of people are finding fruitful occupation. At the meeting the question arose as to what would become of the young men and young women in the Porcupine section, one of the most prosperous in Canada and possibly in the whole civilized world. Mr. John Knox, general superintendent of the Hollinger mine, made the statement that that mine had been in existence for a quarter of a century. Mr. Knox considered it was the duty of the administration of the mines primarily to find employment for the young people in the Timmins district, for the sons of those men who had given many years of good service. I say that it would be unfair to Canadians if we were to entice people from other countries to come to Canada, unless we found it possible to give to our present population plenty of fruitful occupation, also means to build homes and the opportunity to live as they would like to live.
A few days ago I happened to be present to witness the progress of a great movement which, I believe, is a step in the right direction. I never like to make comparisons between provinces, because after all we are all Canadians. However I happened to be in the province of Quebec and to witness a trainload of men being sent to the new settlement in northern Quebec. When I looked at those men I thought to myself that history was being written in big black letters; that our present civilization was trying to rectify conditions and to place back into its proper setting that part of the population which should never have gone into the urban centres. Later on I went to the Abitibi section, to Timiskaming, and to lake St. John. There I saw what the government was doing for these settlers. Not that I am in love with too much paternalism. Some might be inclined to ask what has become of the pioneer spirit of the Loyalists who colonized Ontario, and my ancestors who colonized the north shore of the St. Lawrence river. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that their descendants have just as much courage as their forefathers, but they are facing a different situation to-day, and in the new centres of colonization we now find the government, providing employment, building churches, Protestant and Catholic, paying
the priests and ministers, building schools, all out of the provincial treasury. I have been a settler myself; I know the struggles that these people must go through until they begin to prosper on their new holdings, and I am speaking of them to-night because' I want parliament to be fully seized of their situation. I believe there is hope in the present situation. Humanity has suffered much in the last five 'years, and I want to give all due credit to the late Prime Minister. Nobody can accuse him of being asleep at the switch for he has worked twenty-four hours a day for the last five years. But just the same there is not a Canadian who is satisfied with the present situation. We are all wanting a solution of our problems, and we know that it cannot be brought about by any simple formula. But when you see provincial governments working in cooperation with the federal government and know that this government is fully seized of the situation-and we all remember its back to the land movement of a few years ago-I believe, knowing our fine population as I do, that if we will all combine our energies our country wfill eventually emerge from this depression, regain the prosperity she enjoyed in previous years, and experience fuller days of progressiveness, of self-reliance, and of a fuller life for the whole nation.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to speak from this comer of the house this evening. It is a new experience for me to address the house, and I venture upon it with diffidence and modesty. But we feel that we in this part of the chamber have a new philosophy to offer.
My sympathy is with the government in the problems with which it is faced, and I should like to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) most heartily upon the very able manner in which he has put forward his ideas, but at the same time I feel that they will not solve the problem with which we are faced, that of scarcity in the midst of plenty. As was said by the great Shakespeare, "The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars but in ourselves, that we are underlings." It has been said by the Dean of Canterbury that the social crediters embody the best aspirations of the Conservatives, the Liberals, and the socialists, and so I would say that we are sitting in a very enviable position in this house inspired as we are to carry out the great ideals enunciated by the Dean of Canterbury.
The nations that feed and clothe and shelter their inhabitants will stand out as shining examples to the rest of the world.
254	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Hayhurst
We believe a new age is being ushered in, and because of that we believe Canada should adopt the new idealism or the new economics, that we may usher in a new philosophy whereby this enigma of poverty in the midst of plenty may'be solved.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has said that this government does not believe it can end unemployment by its own unaided efforts. We believe that also. We contend that we should combine our forces against scarcity. The minister also said that the relief camps should be closed. We also think they should be closed and the men who have been living in them should be given a more decent and a better standard of living. We are all of us striving for a higher standard of living, and that is what the social credit people stand for.
Speaking at Kingston the Minister of Labour used these words, as reported in the Whig Standard:
Unemployment is not going to vanish in the twinkling of an eye, and it is impossible for any government to deal with it on that basis. Recovery rests on the primary industries and on raising the purchasing power of the workers in those industries.
In reply to that I would say that unemployment has increased even in times of industrial activity. As the president of the Bank of Nova Scotia said in his annual address to the shareholders, we cannot begin to absorb the army of unemployed, even if we went back to the degree of industrial activity that we had in 1929. We are firmly convinced that unemployment has been brought upon the world by the industrial and mechanical genius of man; that this scientific age has brought us into a new era, and that we need a new economics to solve the problem of unemployment.
That large numbers of people will never be able to find work is probably true. We do not think work is necessarily a virtue. We believe men and women should have more time to think out their problems and leisure is something for which we should all strive. Our scientists have been working day and night in order that we might be relieved of unnecessary labour and drudgery, and we believe in ushering in an age of leisure, rather than an age of employment as it is often spoken of, believing that man must not necessarily work, but that he should be paid, and that instead of employment we should use the term "empayment." We believe everyone should be paid. We believe in citizenship; that men and women, boys and girls, are the real asset of any nation; that we should do what we can in this great
. 
dominion to release them from the idea of scarcity, from the fear regarding to-morrow's dinner pail, and that they should be provided with housing accommodation such as is recommended in the resolution now before us. We have the materials, the lumber, and the men. All the materials are at hand, and all we need to do is to put them together.
The present monetary system is suffering from a lack of tickets. It is a system controlled by a certain policy which is in the interests of financiers. We believe we should control the money policy for the welfare of mankind. It does seem ridiculous to me that we, an intelligent people, should allow financial autocracy to rule us when all we need to do is to control this ticket system.
The Minister of Labour has said that we should not spend our way into chaos. We believe it is ridiculous, of course, to think of debt creation, if that is what he means by spending our way into chaos. Chaos was a a great word used by the Liberal party in the campaign in Alberta, where their slogan was. "Vote for King or chaos," and I suppose that is what the minister is thinking of. We believe the debt creating system, as it is understood to-day by modern financiers, leads to nothing but chaos. If we control our credit we can give everyone the necessities of life. We have solved the problem of production and the only trouble to-day is that we have not solved the problem of paying people. We believe every individual as a citizen of Canada is entitled to be paid, whether at work or not. Lord Bryce said that money power was man's most dangerous and insidious enemy. Many of our great economists, including Arthur Kitson and some of the great German economists, have said that international money power as controlled by the international bank of settlements at Geneva .must cease, otherwise we shall always live in poverty, or large numbers of our people will be living in poverty with their children in neglect. I have been a school teacher most of my lifetime and I realize that many of our young people have no opportunities whatever under the present silly system. Our young people should be our real wealth and they should be given opportunities in life. The older people should be pensioned off. We believe real wealth consists of goods, lands and property and that should be monetized if we are to use the term " money."
There seems to be dawning a tremendous era of money manipulation. For instance, in England they are planning, to manipulate their money system in order to bring into

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Hay hurst
being a two billion dollar war machine. Where will they get the money from? We know it will be merely a debt creating system upon which they will be expected to pay interest. Such subtle money manipulations will lead ultimately to disaster. We believe we are at the crossroads of history and we must go forward or go under. We have struggled for political liberty; we have struggled for personal liberty, but we feel we are endangered to-day by the possibility of financial slavery. We should struggle for financial liberty and freedom; that is our business here. We are ready to cooperate with anyone who will look into the future and endeavour to free mankind from this slavery to the banks.
Unemployment has been mentioned this evening. It would seem that the proof of scientific progress is the increasing mastery of man over nature in order to put men out of work. Ideas sometimes can become as powerful as chains of steel. As we see the situation, the world to-day is in the grip of a nightmare and unless we break away from this evil spell of false convictions, the nightmare will continue. We feel that to-day we have a wastage of youth, a wastage of commodities and a wastage of machines. Hon. members may not believe this, but I ask them to go out to Alberta and see the tractors lying idle behind the barbed wire fences. There are more machines idle to-day -than there are idle men. We are talking about unemployment but we should be thinking of putting our machines to work and giving our people more liberty. What is physically possible should be financially possible. To-day we feel that the big fish are eating the little fish; the little fish eat the minnows and sometimes I think the farmers in the west are the minnows.
We agree that the slums should be abolished. I have before me a little article on the abolition of these slums. In reviewing the progress made in housing, one hon. member mentioned Great Britain. Sir Halton Young has said that although between 1918 and 1933 the number of inhabited houses had increased by 1,363,000, this did not produce the expected filtering of population and the automatic disappearance of the slums and overcrowding, the reason of course being that the slum tenants could not pay the rents. This slum problem is a good example of the glaring defects in our economic system. There is something peculiarly dreadful in the thought of these acres of squalor in the large cities. It is not only in the large cities, because in the rural areas of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta you will find some of the most appalling conditions. You will find men and women living in habitations not fit for their dogs.
Such a condition should rankle in the national conscience; it should rankle in the minds of all good thinking people. We must do something to solve this problem. I do not th'ink there is one hon. member who does not believe we have the labour, the materials and the mechanical skill necessary to do this work. In fact, we have all the resources at our command, but still the slums remain. It is only a matter of a little bookkeeping, but because of our curious habit of charging capital costs into prices we cannot build houses to rent at amounts within the spending power of the poorer classes. However, by adjusting costs and distributing national dividends to the tenants by means of new material created for the purpose and not issued as a debt to the banks we could solve the slum problem with the greatest of ease. What did Major Douglas say with regard to the control of finance as we have it to-day? We have two systems, the productive and the financial, and this is what Major Douglas has to say:
Most people thought that, in some mysterious way, when wealth was produced money was produced. On the contrary, we could produce real wealth of every kind until we were black in the face and we would not produce one penny of purchasing power. This separation of the economic system into a production system and a financial system was the first step toward an understanding of the situation.
It is a delusion that money of itself is something of worth-the real wealth is goods. People have the idea that money is something born of blood and tears, and therefore it is valuable. Being a new speaker, I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the house, but I should like to give a few words of Arthur Kitson upon this great subject:
The post-war period ushered in an entirely new era, unlike any former period of the world's history; a period in which man's inventive genius has placed within mankind's reach boundless wealth, sufficient for every inhabitant of this planet to enjoy life without encroaching upon supplies needed by any of his fellows; a period in which nature's powers have been harnessed to machinery for furnishing all the necessaries and most of the so-called luxuries of life. And yet amidst all this abundance, we are inundated with myriads of starving, ragged people living in hovels, all because our officials have not the intelligence to see that the old economic theories have become fallacies, the old monetary and banking systems unworkable, and that just as our productive methods to which we owe this age of plenty have been revolutionized, so our entire economic system must be reorganized.

Being of a retiring nature, I am
always hesitant about entering any debate. It certainly was not my intention to say anything on the resolution presented by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), but after listening to his presentation and the
256	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Leader
words .from our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I am inclined to think this is an opportune time for any member who represents a part of this dominion to bring his views before the house.
I am not going to discuss a number of questions, many of which have been brought before us this afternoon and evening, but I do want to say something about a certain matter with which I am very intimately connected. At the same time I want to offer friendly if not valuable suggestions to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). I take it that this policy of the present government is only in its formulative stage, and that they will welcome any suggestions that any member can bring forward which will help them in drafting a proper policy.
I think I should be remiss in my duties if I did not take advantage of this opportunity to speak to-night, and the particular phase of the subject which I would discuss is the farm placement plan. Hon. members may not know it, but I would inform them that I am what is called a working farmer. I have lived all my life on the farm and I should know something about the conditions. Now as regards unemployment, that has never given me very much concern personally; I was always able to find employment on the farm; in fact, the problem that bothered me was to find time to perform the work I had set before me. At the same time I realize that unemployment is the greatest problem we have to deal with in Canada to-day, and so I will say something about the farm placement plan which I believe was inaugurated by the late government.
As hon. members know, this policy provides So a month for any man willing to take a chance and work for a farmer. Originally I believe it provided $5 a month also for the farmer, to compensate him for the man's board, but that was discontinued; I do not know why, but I have heard it suggested that it had become a racket. I do not know whether that is true, but I have made inquiries in my own province, and so far as Manitoba is concerned I am informed by the government that there was very little abuse connected with the farm placement scheme as it affected that province. But even if a little abuse did exist, all the benefits that have been derived from that policy counterbalance any abuses that could possibly creep in. At any rate, the policy of paying the farmer So a month was discontinued and so we have only the policy of $5 a month for the man who will work on the farm. From my information I gather that this is the most effective and most economical

form of farm relief; that was the information disclosed to the convention of United Farmers at Portage la Prairie last fall.
I would therefore submit a suggestion to the Minister of Labour, who referred to this subject this afternoon; indeed, I would not have entered the debate had he not said that the government could pay $10 a month to these men and save money in connection with the expenses involved in the maintenance of the relief camps. In my opinion we could pay a man $10 a month to work for a farmer and the farmer $10 a month for boarding the man! Some may question the wisdom of allowing the farmer $10 a month for board. Well, I come from a farm and I know conditions there; as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) suggested there are many farmers who cannot afford to board a man, and board is worth at least $10 a month even on a farm. That is why I suggest that the government, when taking this policy into consideration, should not only pay $10 to the man going to work on the farm but also pay the farmer $10 for boarding the man.
We learned at the convention at Portage la Prairie that approximately 4,000 farm hands were placed on farms in Manitoba last year. I believe we could place 10,000 farm hands among the farmers of that province if the scheme I suggest were carried out. To those who would object to paying the farmer $10 a month in compensation for board, I would point out that this would add that much' more purchasing power to the farmer, whose purchasing power was never at a lower ebb; and this money would be spent in the local districts to pay store bills and to carry on business in their own districts throughout Canada, instead of the money going, as most of it now does, to some wholesale firm or some other concern where it is more centralized and not distributed over the whole country, as it is very desirable it should be.
Now, how would this affect unemployment? I think it would cure unemployment in so far as you would keep these men out of the cities. And I would not limit this to the man who never was on a farm in his life. Under the . present form of relief these men must declare, in the document they are required to sign, that they have no homes; that they have no places to go; that they have no money; and then they are taken care of. If they have made money during the summer they are precluded from enjoying the benefits of this scheme. If they are under sixteen years of age they are prohibited from enjoying its benefits. I had a case up at Portage la Prairie where the farmer appealed to me, saying that his

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
application for a sixteen year old boy was turned down, although he was, the farmer told me, one of the best men he ever had on his farm. The boy had no other place to go; his parents were on relief; and just because the farmer put in his age at sixteen the application was denied. I am glad to say that after the matter was taken up with the Manitoba government, they in turn perhaps having submitted it to this government at Ottawa, he was allowed to stay on the farm where the farmer thought he was the best man he ever had.
There should be more elasticity about these applications. I had another case submitted to me in which a farmer's application was turned down simply because the man had made $120 during the summer. That should not be held against a man. If he was industrious enough to get out and earn $120 during the summer he had a perfect right to be taken care of during the winter time; and I know from information I got that $60 of the money he had earned had gone to his father and mother to help them. Yet his application was turned down. I have not heard whether the government has since been able to accept that application, but I think it is a crime if a man who is willing to work is not allowed to take advantage of this plan.

I looked forward with a great deal of interest to the speech of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). I think we all recognized his sincerity and his ability. I was glad that he suggested that none of us should impute motives to others; that we should all recognize that we are anxious, each in his own way, to solve this problem. But he further suggested that certain people in this house were rather inclined to look to some set panacea. I submit to him that we must have some working hypothesis, some working theory, in order to place things in their right perspective. I think if anyone has a working theory of that kind the minister has it, the old Liberal theory of allowing things to work out in their own way, so in holding that view his position is no more to be commended than that of some of us who may believe in a definitely planned economy.
The minister says, and I have no doubt whatever that he quite believes, that the national credit should not be given precedence over human needs. By "national credit" I do not think he means at all what my friends to my left mean by it; he means that our position in the money markets of the world should not be impaired. But while that is a very laudable desire, he suggests that we should not allow that consideration to blind

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Woodsworth
us or prevent us taking action in order to meet the pressing needs of the people. I agree with the minister in that; I think that is absolutely true, and it is because I believe in that statement I insist that the government should now face this situation, because by delaying week after week and month after month we are simply making matters worse. Think of these young fellows who have been in the camps, unemployed, for three, four and five years. I take it that this question should be dealt with at once; that their welfare should be given first consideration, whatever that requires. I take it that this is really what we have in mind when we say human needs should come first. Whatever it may cost us and whatever our other financial commitments may be, we must care for the people of this country.
The minister states his faith in and reliance upon the natural channels of private and corporate investment. Well, personally I am sure he is doomed to disappointment. We have too long trusted those so called natural channels of private and corporate investment, and they have failed us. It was by trusting them in the past that we got into this chaotic condition, and merely continuing to trust them is not going to get us out of it. We must recognize, if we are to carry out the principle that human needs must have priority, that we must begin at once to meet the needs of the million people who are now on relief. Those needs may be met not by giving more adequate relief than is being given to-day, but by setting the men at real work, at certain types of work which are needed in this country and which would greatly enhance the real wealth of the nation.
Other countries have adopted some of the projects that are mentioned by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). In this country we have sacrificed our forest wealth. As I was thinking of this to-day I went to my files and found a diagram which I wish I could show everyone, depicting the situation in British Columbia. When man entered British Columbia some seventy years ago he found 125,000,000 acres of forest stands containing 1,500,000,000,000 feet board measure of timber. Prior to 1918, according to the conservation commission here at Ottawa, fire had destroyed about 665,000,000,000 feet board measure; in the seventeen years from 1918 to 1935 fire 12739-171
destroyed another 230,000,000,000 feet board measure, making a total of 895,000,000,000 feet board measure destroyed by fire, or considerably more than half the entire timber resources of British Columbia. It was said that the administration at that time did not feel that they had the finances necessary to give adequate fire protection. Then this diagram goes on to show the enormous losses through logging wastes, insects, rot, wind and so on. According to the forest branch there is left only 350,000,000,000 feet board measure of workable timber, of which only 111,000,000,000 feet board measure is accessible, according to the statement of the chief forester.

The life and activities of their great commercial and industrial men do not greatly differ from the life and activities of industrial men in our country-nor does the financial man-banker and organizer of industry differ so much from those that perform this service in other countries. There are privileges and luxuries that our financial leaders buy. In the Soviet Union these privileges and luxuries are given to him by the people. They honour service. Honour, appreciation and trust of comrades spur and inspire men to plan and work for the common good of all. Man cannot exploit his fellowman. There is no unemployment in the Soviet Union. Conditions are improving very rapidly. Everyone is tremendously enthusiastic. The health of all is cared for by the state. Pasteur, the great French scientist, said, "The future belongs to science and woe to the nations that close their eyes to this fact." The Soviet government is building a gigantic structure on the solid rock of science and research. For this reason there now remains not a vestige of doubt as to the future success of the Soviet Union.
I give that as an example of a nation which has deliberately planned its life and has used the resources at its command to minister to the needs of the nation. I am not sure how they have financed. Their banking system is rather complicated. But they have controlled their own credit and have had natural resources at their disposal.
In this connection I should like to quote a statement by Stuart Chase in the January issue of Common Sense. Speaking of developments in Russia he said:
Occasionally, I answer them by telling them about Russia in 1927. In that year, I spent some time in the offices of the Gosplan in Moscow, watching a thousand technicians prepare the charts and figures for the first five-year plan. It was proposed to invest the equivalent of thirty billion dollars _ in new capital improvements-dams, transmission lines, railways, factories, apartment houses, oil wells, schools, coal mines, steel plants. Having a "sound" business training back of me, I was perplexed and a little sceptical. Russia was a poor country. She had no capital, no borrowing power, not a nickel of credit. "Where are you going to get the money?" I asked'. Ossinski, one of the best statisticians alive, regarded me with pity. "You should learn, my friend, to look under the veil of money at the real world. Wait and see." Five years later, in 1933, behold the dams, the transmission lines, the factories, the apartment houses, standing solidly-thirty billions worth, as planned. No money, no credit, no confidence, no profit, no "incentive"-yet there they were.
How can you explain that, Mr. Businessman? Your oracles and taboos do not permit of any such performance. But three superior forces do permit it, namely:

Russia had the labour and the resources; she managed to import technical skill to add to her own not inconsiderable stock. The three cardinal factors for the creation of wealth were present. The power dams and factories rose. About them she threw a film of rubles, created as the tangible wealth was gradually created. The rubles only shadowed what the real agents were producing. Wealth came first and money came second. For new public industries in the United States, we have the unused labour of the unemployed, materials in abundance, and a plethora of technical skill. If they can be linked up, a huge amount of new wealth is ours for the taking.
To a certain extent I think I agree with the analysis offered 'by my social credit friends, and with the phrase which they are so fond of using, that what is physically possible is financially possible. I believe that is sound reasoning. However I cannot agree with their theory as to how this is to be done. Fundamentally, what is physically possible is financially passible. We can do it, if we really set our minds to it. In this article Stuart Chase states:
The first question which comes to mind is how new industries have been monetized in the past. In the last century, scores of industries made their appearance, and slid into the financial picture-railroads, bicycles, motor cars, bath tubs, radios, aeroplanes. Where did they get the money? Most business men can tell you only that they borrowed it from banks or investors.
Then he goes on to say that we can finance, just as banks have financed in the past. He states, however, that there have to be some new rules in the game. He suggests three: first, the use of income tax on the higher brackets as a prime method for financing public business. As I have said before, as long as there is wealth in this country, as long as there are people drawing large incomes from the wealth of this country, there is no reason why any single unemployed man should suffer. I would call that to the attention of the minister and if he means, as I think he does, that human needs must come first, then the welfare of these unemployed men must be looked after, even though it may mean very heavy taxation on those whose incomes come within the higher brackets. The second rule that Mr. Chase suggests is the use of non-interest bearing revolving funds of publicly created credit for additional financing of public works. Why not? If the banks can extend credit for profit, the nation surely ought to be in a position to do this in order to meet real human needs. Further this housing scheme might very readily become self-liquidating. Why should we not use national credit for such a purpose?
And thirdly Mr. Chase suggests the socialization of money and credit to prevent sabotage by private bankers, and to keep compound interest in its place. There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that this large group to my left is an indication that the people are insisting that something should be done to meet the real needs of the people. It may be that we cannot meet these needs in the way that the social crediters advocate. Personally I cannot follow their arguments, but nevertheless I think the principle that they hold, and that we in this part of the house hold, that the needs of the people are paramount, is fundamentally true. I take it that the government now have to decide whether they will place financial interests, the service of the debt and so on, in first place, or whether they will place first adequate provision for the needs of the people. I am glad that we have been permitted to have this discussion so early in the session. As the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has stated, the plans of the government are in a formative stage, and we offer these suggestions to them in the hope that they may see fit to take advantage of the opportunity which the people of this country have accorded them.

The resolution, as I look at it, resolves itself into a suggested remedy to take people off the dole and put them back into remunerative employment. The plan for housing, building, reconstruction, renovation, slum clearance, land settlement, reforestation and so forth, is only incidental. Therefore it behooves us to deal for a few moments with the unemployment situation.
In much of the discussion to-day we have heard about slum districts and crowded areas, and about sickness and disease. These conditions are more or less confined to the cities, and throughout the discussion the western farmer has more or less been left out of the picture. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hayhurst), however, has spoken along that line. I am wondering whether the western farmer who lives with his wife and children in perhaps a one-room shack, or in one of two or three rooms, should not have some consideration in a scheme of this sort.
There is one question I should like to ask in connection with the entire discussion, and

perhaps it might be called the proverbial question:	Where is all the money coming
from?
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) in the second part of his resolution suggests that the money might be borrowed on a lower rate structure. I would like to point out that the entire discussion which has ensued upon this resolution has revolved about the present financial system. The logic of all the speeches has been an attempt to run our twentieth century civilization within an eighteenth century financial structure.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) has made the statement that for five years we have been trying to deal with the unemployment emergency. That is just the trouble; we have been dealing with unemployment as an emergency problem. We have not regarded the unemployment situation as being the result of some fundamental principle that is in error. Perhaps it might startle some hon. members if I were to suggest that we are not in a business depression. I might suggest that we are in a stoppage or short-circuiting of our laws of progress. 1 think all will agree that in no matter what field of science we delve there are certain laws of harmony to be found which must work one with the other. Take astronomical science and let us imagine for a moment that the stars in the heavens would say, "Well, boys, we have been going along at this rate for a good many millions of years; let us stop or turn round and go the other way." Something in the nature of a catastrophe would happen, and the same thing is true of mechanical science, physical science or any other branch of science. Yet it seems to me that we have overlooked this fact with regard to the science, if I may put it in that way, or the laws of progress. The age has progressed to a point where we need a new economic system that will care adequately for this very highly progressive and productive age. We are attempting to straddle with one foot in an ox cart and the other in an aeroplane. I should like to read a short quotation from a paper entitled To-day and To-morrow, published in Edmonton. In the issue of January 13, the editor says in part:
Public, or non-productive works, involving borrowing, will provide wages, but those wages must be taken by taxation from those engaged in productive work. This is a method of sharing the poverty of the people, and does not divide up, share, or make available, the machine-made abundance. There is, obviously, only one way out of the difficulty.
If we decide to keep the machines, then we must set up a method of giving people the wages of the machines which do their work. Incomes must be based on wealth produced and not on human labour performed.

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Hansell
I should like to refer a little later to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) with which I heartily agree. I admire his splendid spirit in making those remarks. I should like to quote from a little book entitled From Debt to Prosperity, by J. Crate Larkin. Speaking of the present world crisis the author says:
Of the present world crisis Major Douglas has written, "the break-down of the present financial and1 social system is certain." A comparatively short period will probably serve to decide whether we are to master the mighty economic and social machine that we have created, or whether it is to master us;
I want to emphasize the next few words. I continue:
-and during that period a small impetus from a body of men* who know what to do and how to do it, may make the difference between yet one more retreat into the dark ages, or the emergence into the full light of a day of such splendor as we can at present only envisage dimly.
On his return to England after visiting Canada last July, Major Douglas spoke at a banquet given in his honour on his return. The Calgary Herald of July 20 contains the following article:
Calling for a big electoral compaign in the United Kingdom to break the bankers' monopoly of credit, Major C. H. Douglas at a banquet given ini his honour on his return from Canada declared the world was facing an economic crisis of such magnitude that the next five years would fix the future of this planet for hundreds of years to come.
"Either the outcome must be the beginning of a virtual new epoch of economic freedom," he said, "or else there will be catastrophe and loss of all the freedoms and privileges on which the British empire has hitherto prided itself."
I wonder whether in the phrase in my first quotation, "During that period a small impetus from a body of men who know what to do and how to do it," I cannot see the little body of men who sit around me. Speaking to this resolution, the Prime Minister said that he desired cooperation and constructive criticism; that he was willing to accept any light upon any given subject that would enable the present administration to manage affairs in the interests of the people. I wish to say that hon. members sitting in this corner admire that spirit. I ask hon. members: How many of you have constructive criticisms to make? How many of you have suggestions of help instead of hindrance, suggestions of construction instead of destruction to make? We in this corner of the house desire to help by suggestions which may enlighten matters a little. We desire to help the. present administration to solve the problems that confront us in this parliament.
I suggest that three things are absolutely necessary: first, we must have an absolute and correct diagnosis of the disease. While we are not debating the speech from the throne, perhaps I may refer to it for a moment. I suggest that there was nothing in it to indicate the exact disease. In thinking over the speeches which have been made to-day, I doubt whether they would indicate to us the disease. The first thing necessary for the present administration to do is to diagnose and arrive at the proper disease. The next thing necessary is to discover the remedy to be applied. I have heard several statements made to-day, and in other days, concerning action. We are told that we need action; that we want action, but what we want is the proper kind of action. Third, we need a correct application of the proper remedy. We in this corner desire to contribute to the discovery of the disease, to the suggestion of a proper remedy and to throwing some light upon the proper application of the remedy. We do not desire to see any administration fail. We have no political axe to grind and we trust that the present administration will prove valuable to the country and that within a very few years this country may be taken out of the position in which it stands to-day, on the brink of chaos, to a place of economic, commercial and industrial security.

I am sorry if my remarks have been incorrectly interpreted. We do not desire to criticize destructively but to offer constructive criticism. And now, Mr. Speaker, I will close. By profession I am a clergyman, one of only three, I believe, in the present parliament. Now, as a clergyman, I marry people to make them happy; as a clergyman, I bury people when they are dead. A few months ago we witnessed, I think I can say, the pre-nuptials in the glorious election; I believe last week we perhaps arrived at the place where we witnessed the marriage ceremony, and hon. members opposite have begun to sail the seas of political matrimony in perfect harmony. How they do love one another! I offer them my sincere wishes, as I offer many young couples health, happiness and prosperity and, of course, the proverbial "May all your troubles be little ones." We desire to contribute something to their happiness and welfare; but I do trust-and I am saying this in all seriousness-that in the next five years I shall not have to suffer the embarrassment of having to take part in the funeral service.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): I shall detain the house but a few moments. I wish to congratulate my old friend the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) upon retaining his old time ability to draft an omnibus resolution which would permit the house to discuss almost anything under the sun, also upon his manner of presenting his resolution and upon the general tone and temper of the debate. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) contributed constructively; but naturally, oecupy-

ing a seat on this side of the house, I listened with great pride to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Plaxton), in his maiden speech. The house gave him the usual respectful hearing accorded a first effort, and I feel sure that everyone, regardless of which side of the house he sat on, was pleased, that the hon. gentleman acquitted himself so well. May I also say that in my opinion, as the Hansard of this house of to-day is read in future years, it will be generally conceded that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in his maiden speech made a notable contribution indeed. In fact, the debate as a whole has been on a very high level, if one excepts the somewhat partisan remarks of the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps). There is evident in the house a sincere desire on the part of all members to contribute something constructive toward the solution of problems, the existence of which we all recognize, and in connection with which we all assume our due responsibility for offering something, during the period of our presence here, to bring about improvement.
I only desire to say one or two words by way of information with respect to last session's housing act which has been discussed by several speakers. The hon. member for North Winnipeg was rather reproachful of the previous government and of this one as well, because greater progress had not been made. He spoke very disparagingly of the fact that less than a million dollars has yet been advanced out of the ten millions appropriated by parliament for this purpose. Of course, the less than a million advanced does involve five times that amount of construction. One should bear that in mind, and it is well also to bear in mind that while the legislation was passed in July of last year, we were already entering upon a general election. The legislation depended for its successful operation upon acceptance, by a variety of interests, of various responsibilities under the terms of the law.
Business interests generally are not inclined to assume new obligations just created by an expiring parliament. There was very definitely a waiting tendency on the part both of those who were expected to supply part of the funds, and of the construction industry generally in relation to the dominion housing act. The present government found that condition on coming into office, but it has decided that the housing act now on the statute books is worth a fair trial. No one in the house would claim perfection for it. I am sure the sponsors of it would not. We certainly do not regard it as perfect, but we do

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Dunning
believe that the experience which the government and the house and the country generally may gain by operating it in its present terms will give us the surest possible lead as to the manner in which it may be improved and made more effective. The number of applications coming in is steadily increasing. The number of loaning institutions, life insurance companies and the like, who are taking advantage of its provisions, signing the agreements provided for in the law, is increasing. Some companies are even advertising for business under the terms of the act.
Someone mentioned the desirability of widening the terms of the law in order to create machinery whereby renovation and repair of existing properties might be made possible. Whatever merit there may be in such an idea, it is very doubtful if the machinery of the dominion housing act is the best means of effecting that end. We are watching very carefully the experience in the United States with respect to legislation of this character, that is legislation having to do with the repair and renovation of existing properties and also with respect to slum clearance. In the discussion last year it became quite apparent that no one expected the present housing act to effect what is described as slum clearance. That is a far greater and wider problem than the provision of new moderate priced houses.
As to the other subjects discussed, reforestation and the like, I can only repeat what I said a day or two ago with respect to the supplementary estimates, that each department of the government and each minister are now studying with the utmost care the possibility of providing productive public works expenditures. Perhaps I should not have used the term "public works." What I mean is expenditures to create employment which will be productive and self-sustaining rather than expenditures of such a type as to create further expenditure. To illustrate: We would like, if we could, to get away, as far as possible -we cannot get away from it altogether-from building that class of building which, while adding to a certain public facility, let us say a post office, does not increase the revenues of that facility one iota but does operate to increase the expense of operation. When you build a fine new post office in a small community, that is merely the commencement of the expense in connection with it, because for ever after you must keep it up; you must clean it; you must provide caretakers with salaries and so forth to look after it. That is an illustration of what I call relatively unproductive public expenditures, and I know those
who have served in previous governments will agree with me that it is rather difficult to provide a sufficiency of the other type of public expenditure. That question is engaging the attention of all the members of the government at the present time, and I think it is a little early in the session for the hon. member for North Winnipeg to reproach us so bitterly because we have not now, within two days of the conclusion of the debate on the address, brought down a full-fledged program to solve all the problems to which he referred.
We know the country is expecting much of this parliament; it has a right to. We will attempt to discharge our responsibilities. And we appreciate the manner in which hon. members generally have discussed the resolution now before the house. Probably the purpose of the resolution has been served by the discussion which has taken place. Perhaps my hon. friend who moved it will not agree with me, but to my mind the great advantage of these private members' resolutions is that the government is given an opportunity to learn publicly the constructive ideas brought here by every member of the house, no matter from what part of the country he may come or to what particular party he may belong. That is a great advantage. As to whether it is desirable to have a vote, of course that is in the hands of the mover of the resolution.

In the eleven years I have been in the house I have never before exercised this privilege of closing the debate, and I shall be only a few minutes. But I am dissatisfied and disappointed to-night at the reply offered in the name of Liberalism 'by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). Let me teill him that ten years ago, long before he came to the house, I presented a resolution here for an employment commission after the fashion of Senator Couzen's
266	COMMONS
Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Church
inquiry into unemployment on behalf of the United States senate. Down there they get the senate to pass things: they do not take three weeks' holiday, doing everything by fits and starts. I may tell my hon. friend that his government voted us down when we asked them three or four sessions running what they would do for unemployment. Mr. Heenan was a real working man, and I believe a minister of labour ought to be a real working man. Working men sit in the British parliament, but it seems to me that as Liberal ministers in this country we have professors and chemists and doctors and last, but not least, judges. If any of these four classes of citizens start investigating anything, it is good-by and good-night, and it is put into cold storage at once. As to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), I have every regard for him. I will accept his suggestion and withdraw the motion, though I would rather have it lost on division. There will be another chance another day, but I can tell the Minister of Labour that his announcement in the house will disappoint not only labour throughout Canada but the municipalities who have such a hard time to meet their taxes.
This parliament created a day known as Labour day for the protection of labour. Allow me to say to the Minister of Finance that it is all right to put money in the estimates to protect farmers and fishermen, to protect coal and iron and steel, but have we no right to ask for a measure of protection in the two central provinces where forty-seven per cent of the people of this country have been engaged in industry, and where the homes of so many have been sold? The reply we have had from the young professor from Queen's university might be all right for a mock parliament or an intercollegiate debate, but it is hardly fitting to be addressed to the high court of parliament. As I said before, I admire the nature of the real Liberalism which inspired the miners of Cornwall to march to London town on behalf of Trelawney, in protest against the tyranny of King James II. I admire the spirit of the freeholders of Buckingham in supporting Hampden against the tyranny of Charles Stuart. But I am not in love with the academic Liberalism of the young Minister of Labour's reply. As I said, it may be all right for a mock parliament, but as addressed to parliament and to the workers of this country I think it is an absurdity. The minister says further that his commission, when it is appointed, will be appointed to coordinate measures to handle unemployment. Who will handle unemployment? Probably a professor of economics. The unemployed will all be dead before they get through with the young minister's program.

The minister says that he is not in favour of public works. Funds voted for public works may have been misspent in the United States, but in England this scheme has 'been a unique success, so much so that England has come out of the depression much better than any other country in the world. The minister is against any scheme of public works; he is in favour of allowing private and corporate business to expand employment. Let me ask this young * minister if he is aware of what the oil ring are doing now, working their employees sixty-three hours a week as a result of the references to the supreme court. These sweatshops are doing a land office business now. They were shown up by the price spreads inquiry, that did something for the working classes of this country. For the last two or three weeks the oil ring have been working their employees sixty-three hours a week, and nine hours cm Sunday. Where is the sweat shop and the alien labour laws? I am going to find out whether or not this department is functioning, because we want some measure of protection for the industrial workers of Canada. They are not going to be fooled any longer. We are not going to have some measure of protection for some classes in the community and no protection for others. I am for protection first, last and all the time for all the people of the dominion so that we may have a happy, contented country.
The minister has said that he does not want government finance to retard the expansion of private enterprises. Did you ever hear such nonsense in your life? We had a housing commission which sat for three months, long before the minister was ever a member of this chamber. That commission found that the government should help workingmen build their homes, and I believe that plan will be carried on long after the minister and all the rest of us have passed on. I gave the reason this afternoon, from government reports in England, which may be seen in Hansard to-morrow.
I am very much disappointed, Mr. Speaker, that all these matters have 'been referred to the law courts. Under the Liberal party we had first of all ambassador cure for unemployment; now we have the professor cure; again we are going to have the under secretary cure and last but not least the commission cure. Then there was this reference to the Supreme Court of Canada, judges who know nothing about employment, unemployment or economic matters. Half the trouble we have in this country is due to these economists. Political economy is not an exact science like physics, chemistry or biology. These

Reconstruction Policy-Mr. Church
scientists can argue from facts, 'but our professors and political economists cannot do that. They give their opinions, and they are not worth a scrap of paper, neither is the opinion of the minister with regard to unemployment worth a scrap of paper. Let me tell you, Mr. Minister, that when your commission takes a Cook's tour of Canada and sees conditions in this country, it will open its eyes. If you just go round the city of Toronto or the other industrial cities in this country and see the workingmen losing their homes because of the inefficiency of the Department of Labour you will have something to think about.
This is not the first time I have had something to say about this department. I do not wish to criticize the young minister; he is a young gentleman of great ability, who is very well liked, but I was very much disappointed in listening to a minister of the crown from his place in parliament give an answer such as he gave. If that is all the unemployed have to expect from the present government, unemployment is going to increase by leaps and bounds and you will see a great exodus of our young people. If that is all, these young people, these high school and university students, who are out of work, have to expect, there is not very much for them in this country. Why is parliament called to meet anyway? Are we a lot of office boys or rubber stamps called here to receive an academic reply like that one we heard to-night? I am sorry the industrial worker is not better supported in the house. I intend to ask leave to withdraw this resolution, but I shall do so with great reluctance; I would rather see it lost on division. However, this is only the preliminary hearing at this stage; we shall have a real trial of this case later on.
I hope we will have a proper Liberalism in this country along the lines I have suggested. The Minister of Labour in the previous Liberal government, the Hon. Peter Heenan, was a real workingman who was respected by the working people, but Mr. Heenan told me in the house that there was no unemployment, and that if there was it was a matter for the provinces and municipalities. At that time the government declined to contribute one-third of the cost of relief. They refused the application of the city of Toronto, which I presented in parliament some eight or ten years ago, but later on the government was forced to contribute. When the new government came in it gave fifty per cent of tli6 cost, and I want to commend the new government upon giving seventy-five per cent. I hope before long the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) will be able to go the whole distance and give one hundred per cent.
I have represented an industrial city in many spheres of activity. I have seen the suffering there; I have visited homes in which four generations of families have been out of work. That is an intolerable condition, and something should be done. Unemployment is the great scourge of the human race and it is going to engulf society unless something is done. Things have been going from bad to worse and the unemployed are getting disgusted with the whole performance. Something should be done for Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver and the larger cities of this country, which are suffering so severely from unemployment. Every municipality I have named, from Vancouver to Halifax-and I saw his worship the mayor of Vancouver here a moment ago-has had to put into relief work most of the money raised by taxes. They have not had a dollar to spend on necessary public improvements. This afternoon I referred to the fact that in England they are constructing all the necessary improvements for the next forty years in order to tide people over the depression, and that is going to help the farmers as well.
I hope there will be some reconsideration of this problem between now and the time the estimates come up. The other day the government announced that $25,000,000 would be devoted to reconstruction. The highly industrialized provinces of Ontario and Quebec are paying eighty per cent of the cash taxes of this country, but the industrial workers are getting no protection at all. We have had a commission on maritime rights, a commission on Pacific coast rights and a commission on prairie rights. I tell you the time is coming when we shall have to ask for a commission on the rights of central Canada.
So with great reluctance, Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to withdraw this resolution. I would rather see it lost on division. It. should be lost on division; the government is straight against it. What is the minister going to do about these shark loan companies, incorporated by parliament, which are charging forty per cent on second mortgages in the city of Toronto? What is he going to do about these trust companies, these insurance companies, and so on? I would ask that he use his good offices to see what can be done in that regard. I do not know whether or not they contribute to campaign funds, but they have a way of doing business around parliament. We all saw something

of that in the days of Beauharnois; I know they drove me out of parliament. I would ask the Minister of Finance, also, if he will not use his good offices to stop these foreclosures and give the industrial workers a chance to protect their homes, as the farmers and fishermen have been given chances to protect theirs. With that, Mr. Speaker, I ask your leave to withdraw this resolution.
Motion withdrawn.
